passages.title: Allosteric control of a glycolytic enzyme
paragraphs: Phosphofructokinase-1 catalyses the transfer of a phosphoryl group from ATP to fructose-6-phosphate, giving fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. The reaction is the committed step of glycolysis: once it has happened the sugar cannot easily return to the hexose pool, so the cell regulates this enzyme rather than the steps on either side of it. The enzyme is a tetramer, and each subunit carries a catalytic site for the sugar and a separate regulatory site. ATP is a substrate at the catalytic site, but at higher concentrations it also occupies the regulatory site and lowers the enzyme's affinity for the sugar. Citrate, which accumulates when the citric acid cycle is already well supplied with carbon, binds at that same regulatory site. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate bind elsewhere and raise the affinity for the sugar.

Investigators studied a bacterial form of the enzyme that, under the conditions used, gives a hyperbolic rather than a sigmoidal velocity curve, so that initial rates follow v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Initial velocity was measured over a range of fructose-6-phosphate concentrations at pH 7.4 and 37 °C, with ATP held at 0.10 mM, a concentration low enough to leave the regulatory site unoccupied. The experiment was repeated with each effector present, and an apparent Km and an apparent Vmax were fitted to every curve (Table 1).

A second series used an enzyme in which an arginine of the regulatory site had been replaced by alanine. This protein was indistinguishable from the wild type when assayed with no effector present, and its turnover number was unchanged, but neither ATP at 5 mM nor citrate at 2.0 mM altered its kinetics.

figure.caption: Table 1  Apparent kinetic constants for fructose-6-phosphate with each effector present.

passages.title: Fidelity of DNA replication
paragraphs: A replicative DNA polymerase builds a new strand by adding deoxyribonucleotides to the 3' end of a primer, choosing each one by its ability to pair with the template. Base selection on its own is accurate to about one error in 10⁵ nucleotides added. The same enzyme carries a second active site that hydrolyses the nucleotide it has just added when that nucleotide is mispaired; this activity works in the 3' to 5' direction on the newly made strand and is called proofreading. A separate system, mismatch repair, scans the finished duplex, distinguishes the new strand from the template and excises a tract containing the mismatch so that it can be resynthesised.

Because the three mechanisms act in series, their contributions multiply. Investigators measured the mutation rate of a bacterium whose genome is 4.6 × 10⁶ base pairs, using a reporter gene whose inactivation can be scored on selective plates. Four strains were compared: a wild-type strain, a strain whose polymerase lacks the proofreading site, a strain lacking the mismatch repair system, and a strain lacking both (Table 2). Every culture was grown for the same number of generations without selection before plating.

The investigators noted that both single mutants grew at normal rates, while the double mutant grew more slowly and lost viability over successive subcultures. Sequencing of the reporter gene from the proofreading-deficient strain showed almost entirely single base substitutions, while the reporter from the mismatch-repair-deficient strain carried, in addition to substitutions, frequent insertions and deletions of one or two base pairs within short runs of a repeated base.

figure.caption: Table 2  Measured error rate of each strain.

StrainErrors per base pair replicated
Wild type1 × 10⁻¹⁰
Proofreading-deficient1 × 10⁻⁷
Mismatch-repair-deficient1 × 10⁻⁸
Deficient in both1 × 10⁻⁵

passages.title: Oxygen carriage in the blood
paragraphs: Each haemoglobin tetramer binds up to four molecules of oxygen, one at the haem iron of each subunit. Binding is cooperative: the first oxygen bound shifts the tetramer toward a conformation in which the remaining sites bind more readily, which is what gives the sigmoidal relationship between saturation and oxygen partial pressure. The partial pressure at which haemoglobin is half saturated, the P50, is about 27 mmHg in a healthy adult at rest. A fall in pH, a rise in PCO₂, a rise in temperature and a rise in the concentration of 2,3-BPG each raise the P50, shifting the curve to the right and favouring release of oxygen to the tissues; the opposite changes shift it to the left.

Almost all of the oxygen in blood is carried on haemoglobin, and only a little is dissolved in plasma. The oxygen content of arterial blood, in millilitres of oxygen per decilitre of blood, is content = (1.34 × Hb) × SaO₂ + (0.003 × PaO₂), where Hb is the haemoglobin concentration in g/dL, SaO₂ is the fractional saturation of haemoglobin and PaO₂ is the arterial partial pressure of oxygen in mmHg. The first term is the oxygen bound to haemoglobin and the second is the oxygen in physical solution.

Four adults attending a clinic were studied. Haemoglobin concentration, arterial saturation measured by co-oximetry and arterial oxygen partial pressure are given in Table 3. Subject J was a healthy control. Subject K had iron deficiency anaemia. Subject L had advanced lung disease. Subject M had been rescued from a house fire and had inhaled carbon monoxide, which binds haem with an affinity more than two hundred times that of oxygen and, by occupying some subunits, holds the remaining subunits in the high-affinity conformation.

passages.title: A receptor variant and the restriction point
paragraphs: Most animal cells will not divide unless a growth factor tells them to. The signal is received by a receptor whose cytoplasmic domain is a protein kinase: binding of growth factor brings two receptor molecules together, each phosphorylates the other, and a cascade running through Ras and the mitogen-activated protein kinases ends in transcription of the genes for the D-type cyclins. A cyclin-dependent kinase activated by those cyclins phosphorylates the retinoblastoma protein, which in its unphosphorylated form holds inactive the transcription factors that switch on the genes of DNA replication. Once the retinoblastoma protein is phosphorylated, the cell passes the restriction point in G1 and completes the cycle whether or not growth factor is still present.

A laboratory identified a receptor variant, found in a tumour, in which a short deletion in the extracellular domain lets two receptor molecules associate without growth factor. Cultured fibroblasts were transfected with no construct, with the normal receptor, or with the variant receptor. Each culture was grown to confluence in serum, washed, and then held in serum-free medium for 24 hours. The cells were fixed, their DNA stained, and the proportion in each phase of the cycle determined by flow cytometry (Table 4).

Serum is the usual source of growth factors in culture, so serum-free medium leaves a cell with no mitogenic signal from outside. The investigators confirmed by immunoblotting that the normal and variant receptors were present in similar amounts at the cell surface, and that neither construct altered the total amount of retinoblastoma protein in the cell.

figure.caption: Table 4  Distribution of cells by cycle phase after 24 hours without serum.

passages.title: Transfer of a resistance plasmid
paragraphs: Bacteria acquire genes from one another in three main ways. In transformation, a competent cell takes up DNA from the medium around it. In transduction, a bacteriophage carries host DNA from one cell into the next. In conjugation, a donor builds a pilus that contacts a recipient and passes a copy of a plasmid through the bridge that forms; because the DNA never enters the medium, conjugation proceeds even in the presence of a nuclease that would destroy any free DNA. A plasmid may carry several resistance genes at once, so a single transfer event can convert a susceptible strain into a strain resistant to drugs of two unrelated classes.

A clinical isolate of Escherichia coli carried a plasmid with two resistance genes: one encoding an enzyme that hydrolyses the strained four-membered ring of penicillins, and one encoding a pump that exports tetracycline from the cytoplasm. The isolate was mixed with a plasmid-free recipient strain distinguishable by a chromosomal marker. After 2 hours the recipients were separated and their minimum inhibitory concentrations determined (Table 5). The mating was repeated with a deoxyribonuclease present throughout, and separately the recipient was incubated with purified plasmid DNA and the same nuclease rather than with donor cells.

Growth of the recipient strain was also followed in rich broth. Starting from 1.0 × 10³ cells/mL, it divided once every 30 minutes for the whole period studied, with no detectable lag. Neither the plasmid-free recipient nor the strain that had received the plasmid grew more slowly than the other in drug-free broth, so carrying the plasmid imposed no measurable cost under these conditions.

passages.title: Fuel use during a prolonged fast
paragraphs: An adult at rest oxidises about 300 g of glucose a day, of which the brain takes roughly 120 g. The liver holds about 100 g of glycogen and can release the glucose from it into the blood; skeletal muscle holds about 400 g but lacks the phosphatase needed to export free glucose, so muscle glycogen serves muscle alone. As a fast continues, falling insulin releases adipose tissue lipolysis from inhibition, free fatty acids are mobilised, and the liver converts part of the resulting acetyl-CoA into the ketone bodies acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, which the brain can oxidise.

Oxidation of a fatty acid begins with its activation to a coenzyme A thioester, at a cost of two ATP equivalents. Each round of the oxidation spiral then shortens the chain by two carbons and yields one NADH, one FADH₂ and one acetyl-CoA, except that the last round yields two acetyl-CoA and no further shortening. Taking each NADH as 2.5 ATP, each FADH₂ as 1.5 ATP and each acetyl-CoA oxidised in the citric acid cycle as 10 ATP gives the net yield of a saturated fatty acid of any length.

Six healthy volunteers fasted for 72 hours under observation. Plasma glucose, insulin, free fatty acids and 3-hydroxybutyrate were measured at intervals (Table 6). All six remained well, and in no subject did plasma glucose fall below 3.5 mM. Urinary nitrogen excretion rose over the first two days and then fell, and indirect calorimetry showed that by 72 hours more than four fifths of the energy being expended came from the oxidation of fat.

figure.caption: Table 6  Plasma measurements during a 72 hour fast, mean of six subjects.

passages.title: Recovery of glucose in the proximal tubule
paragraphs: Blood is filtered at the glomerulus at about 125 mL/min in a healthy adult, and the filtrate begins with the same concentration of small solutes as plasma. Essentially all of the filtered glucose is recovered in the proximal tubule. On the basolateral surface of the tubule cell a pump hydrolyses ATP to move three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in, which keeps the intracellular sodium concentration low. On the apical surface, facing the filtrate, a carrier binds sodium and glucose together and takes both into the cell: sodium moves down its electrochemical gradient, and glucose is dragged up its own concentration gradient. Glucose then leaves across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion.

The amount of a solute delivered to the tubule each minute is its filtered load, the product of the filtration rate and the plasma concentration. The carriers have a finite capacity: once the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, which is about 2.0 mmol/min for glucose in an adult, the excess stays in the tubular fluid and appears in the urine. Plasma glucose in a fasting adult is about 5.0 mmol/L.

Investigators perfused isolated segments of proximal tubule and measured glucose uptake across the apical membrane. Uptake was abolished when the sodium in the perfusate was replaced by an impermeant cation, and it did not increase further once the glucose concentration in the perfusate was raised past the point at which the carriers were saturated. A second preparation was used to confirm that the same segments reabsorbed amino acids by carriers that also depend on sodium, and that uptake of both classes of solute was lost together when sodium was removed.

passages.title: An inherited hearing loss
paragraphs: Severe hearing loss present from birth is most often inherited, and in populations of European descent a large share of cases is accounted for by loss-of-function variants in a single gene, encoding the gap junction protein connexin 26. Gap junctions are channels that connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells directly to one another. In the cochlea they link the supporting cells that surround the sensory hair cells, and they provide the route by which the potassium that enters hair cells during transduction is passed back to the fluid of the cochlear duct. Without that route the ion gradients on which transduction depends cannot be maintained, and the hair cells degenerate.

Variants in this gene are recessive: a person with one normal copy hears normally. In one surveyed population 4 of every 10 000 people have hearing loss attributable to this gene, and the population may be treated as being in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium at the locus. Many other genes can also cause non-syndromic recessive hearing loss, so two deaf people are not necessarily homozygous at the same locus.

A clinic reviewed its records. Among 40 families in which both parents heard normally and at least one child was deaf, affected children made up close to a quarter of the children in those sibships, and affected sons and daughters were about equally common. Among couples in which both partners were deaf, most had only deaf children, but in several families every child heard normally. No pedigree in the series showed an affected individual in three successive generations.
